topic: Caught-in or -between hazards: excavations and trenching

notes.front: What is an excavation, in Subpart P of the construction standards?
notes.back: Any man-made cut, cavity, trench or depression in an earth surface, formed by earth removal.
notes.explanation: The definition is broad: a trench is one kind of excavation, and so is any other hole dug by removing earth.
notes.example: A basement hole for a new house, a pit dug to repair a buried valve, or a long pipe trench.
notes.evidence: Excavation means any man-made cut, cavity, trench, or depression in an earth surface, formed by earth removal.
notes.source: 29 CFR 1926.650(b), Definitions (excavations), p. 337

notes.front: What is a trench, in Subpart P?
notes.back: A narrow excavation below ground, narrow in relation to its length; in general deeper than wide, and at most 15 feet wide at the bottom.
notes.explanation: A trench is a kind of excavation defined by its narrow shape and its bottom width.
notes.example: Like a basement dig, but long and narrow, such as a cut 3 feet wide and 6 feet deep for a water main.
notes.evidence: Trench (Trench excavation) means a narrow excavation (in relation to its length) made below the surface of the ground. In general, the depth is greater than the width, but the width of a trench (measured at the bottom) is not greater than 15 feet (4.6 m).
notes.source: 29 CFR 1926.650(b), Definitions (excavations), p. 338

notes.front: What is a cave-in, in Subpart P?
notes.back: Soil or rock separating from an excavation's side, or lost from under a trench shield or support system, and moving suddenly into the excavation.
notes.explanation: The definition adds that the movement is by falling or sliding, in enough quantity to entrap, bury or otherwise injure and immobilise a person.
notes.example: Like a sandcastle wall slumping, but a trench wall that drops tonnes of soil onto a pipe layer.
notes.evidence: Cave-in means the separation of a mass of soil or rock material from the side of an excavation, or the loss of soil from under a trench shield or support system, and its sudden movement into the excavation, either by falling or sliding
notes.source: 29 CFR 1926.650(b), Definitions (excavations), p. 337

notes.front: What is a protective system, in Subpart P?
notes.back: A method of protecting employees from cave-ins, from material falling or rolling from a face or into an excavation, or from collapse of adjacent structures.
notes.explanation: Subpart P names support systems, sloping and benching systems and shield systems among protective systems, and allows other systems that give the necessary protection.
notes.example: Like a hard hat for a whole trench: the sides are cut back, braced or boxed in so the soil cannot reach the workers.
notes.evidence: Protective system means a method of protecting employees from cave-ins, from material that could fall or roll from an excavation face or into an excavation, or from the collapse of adjacent structures.
notes.source: 29 CFR 1926.650(b), Definitions (excavations), p. 337

notes.front: What is sloping (a sloping system)?
notes.back: Protecting employees from cave-ins by cutting the sides of an excavation so they incline away from it.
notes.explanation: Sloping is one of the protective systems Subpart P names; the incline itself is what prevents the cave-in.
notes.example: Like the sides of a bowl rather than a bucket: the walls lean back from the bottom of the dig.
notes.evidence: Sloping (Sloping system) means a method of protecting employees from cave-ins by excavating to form sides of an excavation that are inclined away from the excavation so as to prevent cave-ins.
notes.source: 29 CFR 1926.650(b), Definitions (excavations), p. 338

notes.front: What is benching (a benching system)?
notes.back: Protecting employees from cave-ins by cutting the sides of an excavation into one or more horizontal levels or steps.
notes.explanation: The definition adds that the surfaces between levels are usually vertical or near-vertical.
notes.example: Like sloping, but the wall is cut as a staircase of wide steps instead of one smooth incline.
notes.evidence: Benching (Benching system) means a method of protecting employees from cave-ins by excavating the sides of an excavation to form one or a series of horizontal levels or steps, usually with vertical or near-vertical surfaces between levels.
notes.source: 29 CFR 1926.650(b), Definitions (excavations), p. 337

notes.front: What is shoring (a shoring system)?
notes.back: A structure, such as a metal hydraulic, mechanical or timber system, that supports the sides of an excavation and is designed to prevent cave-ins.
notes.explanation: Shoring holds the existing walls in place, where sloping and benching remove soil to change the wall's shape.
notes.example: Like bookends holding up a row of books, but hydraulic struts pressing timber panels against both trench walls.
notes.evidence: Shoring (Shoring system) means a structure such as a metal hydraulic, mechanical or timber shoring system that supports the sides of an excavation and which is designed to prevent cave-ins.
notes.source: 29 CFR 1926.650(b), Definitions (excavations), p. 338

notes.front: What is a shield system?
notes.back: A structure able to withstand the forces of a cave-in and so protect the employees inside it.
notes.explanation: Unlike shoring, a shield is not described as supporting the walls: it protects the people within it if the walls do fail.
notes.example: Like a steel cage lowered into a trench, with the pipe crew working between its walls.
notes.evidence: Shield (Shield system) means a structure that is able to withstand the forces imposed on it by a cave-in and thereby protect employees within the structure.
notes.source: 29 CFR 1926.650(b), Definitions (excavations), p. 338

notes.front: What is stable rock, in Subpart P?
notes.back: Natural solid mineral material that can be excavated with vertical sides and will remain intact while exposed.
notes.explanation: Stable rock tops the Subpart P hierarchy of soil and rock deposits, ahead of Types A, B and C.
notes.example: Like a road cutting through solid granite whose vertical face stays put, unlike a bank of sand.
notes.evidence: Stable rock means natural solid mineral material that can be excavated with vertical sides and will remain intact while exposed.
notes.source: 29 CFR 1926.650(b), Definitions (excavations), p. 338

notes.front: What is Type A soil?
notes.back: Cohesive soil with an unconfined compressive strength of 1.5 tons per square foot or greater.
notes.explanation: Appendix A gives clay, silty clay, sandy clay and clay loam as examples of cohesive soils, and counts cemented soils such as caliche and hardpan as Type A.
notes.example: Like a firm, dense clay that holds a thumbprint shape, as opposed to loose, running sand.
notes.evidence: Type A means cohesive soils with an unconfined compressive strength of 1.5 ton per square foot (tsf) (144 kPa) or greater.
notes.source: 29 CFR 1926 Subpart P, Appendix A (b), Definitions, p. 344

notes.front: What is Type B soil, by unconfined compressive strength?
notes.back: Cohesive soil with an unconfined compressive strength greater than 0.5 but less than 1.5 tons per square foot.
notes.explanation: Type B also takes in some granular cohesionless soils, such as angular gravel, silt and sandy loam, and most previously disturbed soils.
notes.example: Like Type A clay, but weaker, or like a clay that would be Type A if it were not cracked.
notes.evidence: Type B means: (i) Cohesive soil with an unconfined compressive strength greater than 0.5 tsf (48 kPa) but less than 1.5 tsf (144 kPa)
notes.source: 29 CFR 1926 Subpart P, Appendix A (b), Definitions, p. 344

notes.front: What is Type C soil?
notes.back: Cohesive soil of 0.5 tons per square foot or less; granular soils such as gravel, sand and loamy sand; or submerged or freely seeping soil.
notes.explanation: Type C is the least stable category in the Appendix A hierarchy; the definition also lists submerged unstable rock and some layered systems.
notes.example: Like beach sand, or clay soaked by groundwater seeping out of the trench wall.
notes.evidence: Type C means: (i) Cohesive soil with an unconfined compressive strength of 0.5 tsf (48 kPa) or less; or (ii) Granular soils including gravel, sand, and loamy sand; or (iii) Submerged soil or soil from which water is freely seeping
notes.source: 29 CFR 1926 Subpart P, Appendix A (b), Definitions, p. 345

notes.front: A trench's width, measured at the bottom, is not greater than {{c1::15 feet}}.
notes.explanation: Past that bottom width, the dig is an excavation but not a trench; forms or structures that narrow the gap to 15 feet or less make it a trench again.
notes.evidence: the width of a trench (measured at the bottom) is not greater than 15 feet (4.6 m). If forms or other structures are installed or constructed in an excavation so as to reduce the dimension measured from the forms or structure to the side of the excavation to 15 feet (4.6 m) or less
notes.source: 29 CFR 1926.650(b), Definitions (excavations), p. 338

notes.front: Which of these digs is a trench under Subpart P?
notes.choices:
A) A pit 30 feet square and 8 feet deep for a pump station
B) A graded building pad 1 foot deep
C) A cut 20 feet wide at the bottom and 6 feet deep
D) A cut 4 feet wide at the bottom, 7 feet deep and 200 feet long
notes.back: D: the cut 4 feet wide, 7 feet deep and 200 feet long.
notes.choicesExplained: A and C are wider than 15 feet at the bottom, so they are excavations but not trenches. B is a shallow excavation, not a narrow, deep cut.
notes.explanation: D is narrow in relation to its length, deeper than it is wide, and no more than 15 feet wide at the bottom.
notes.evidence: Trench (Trench excavation) means a narrow excavation (in relation to its length) made below the surface of the ground. In general, the depth is greater than the width, but the width of a trench (measured at the bottom) is not greater than 15 feet (4.6 m).
notes.source: 29 CFR 1926.650(b), Definitions (excavations), p. 338

notes.front: A cave-in includes not only soil separating from an excavation's side but also the loss of soil from under {{c1::a trench shield or support system}}.
notes.explanation: So a shield or support system does not rule out a cave-in: soil moving out from beneath it and into the excavation counts too.
notes.evidence: Cave-in means the separation of a mass of soil or rock material from the side of an excavation, or the loss of soil from under a trench shield or support system, and its sudden movement into the excavation
notes.source: 29 CFR 1926.650(b), Definitions (excavations), p. 337

notes.front: What kinds of protective system does Subpart P name?
notes.back: Support systems; sloping and benching systems; shield systems; and other systems that provide the necessary protection.
notes.explanation: The list ends with an open category, so a system need not be one of the named kinds if it provides the necessary protection.
notes.evidence: Protective systems include support systems, sloping and benching systems, shield systems, and other systems that provide the necessary protection.
notes.source: 29 CFR 1926.650(b), Definitions (excavations), p. 337

notes.front: Every employee in an excavation must be protected from cave-ins by an adequate protective system, except in which two cases?
notes.back: Entirely in stable rock; or under 5 feet deep with a competent person finding no indication of a potential cave-in.
notes.explanation: The 5-foot exception has two conditions: depth alone is not enough without the competent person's examination of the ground.
notes.evidence: Excavations are made entirely in stable rock; or (ii) Excavations are less than 5 feet (1.52m) in depth and examination of the ground by a competent person provides no indication of a potential cave-in.
notes.source: 29 CFR 1926.652(a)(1), Requirements for protective systems, p. 341

notes.front: A trench is 4 feet deep in clay. The competent person sees tension cracks opening along one edge. Must the crew in it have a protective system?
notes.choices:
A) No: any trench under 5 feet is exempt
B) Yes: the competent person found an indication of a potential cave-in
C) No, provided the crew wear helmets
D) Only if the trench is deeper than 20 feet
notes.back: B: yes, because there is an indication of a potential cave-in.
notes.choicesExplained: A ignores the second condition of the exception. C is wrong: helmets are not a protective system against cave-ins. D confuses the depth at which an engineer must design the system.
notes.explanation: The under-5-feet exception applies only when the competent person's examination shows no indication of a potential cave-in; cracks are such an indication here.
notes.evidence: Excavations are less than 5 feet (1.52m) in depth and examination of the ground by a competent person provides no indication of a potential cave-in.
notes.source: 29 CFR 1926.652(a)(1), Requirements for protective systems, p. 341

notes.front: A crew cuts a 9-foot-deep trench entirely in stable rock with vertical sides. What does 1926.652(a) require for cave-in protection?
notes.choices:
A) No protective system, because the excavation is entirely in stable rock
B) A trench shield
C) A design by a registered professional engineer
D) Sloping at 1½ to 1
notes.back: A: no protective system is required.
notes.choicesExplained: D, B and C are protective systems or designs that would be needed in soil; excavations made entirely in stable rock are an exception.
notes.explanation: Stable rock is defined as material that stays intact with vertical sides, and an excavation made entirely in it is excepted from the protective-system requirement.
notes.evidence: Excavations are made entirely in stable rock; or (ii) Excavations are less than 5 feet (1.52m) in depth
notes.source: 29 CFR 1926.652(a)(1), Requirements for protective systems, p. 341

notes.front: When is unstable rock considered stable in Subpart P?
notes.back: When it is secured against caving-in or movement by rock bolts or by another protective system designed by a registered professional engineer.
notes.explanation: The securing, not the rock itself, earns the stable classification.
notes.evidence: Unstable rock is considered to be stable when the rock material on the side or sides of the excavation is secured against caving-in or movement by rock bolts or by another protective system that has been designed by a registered professional engineer.
notes.source: 29 CFR 1926.650(b), Definitions (excavations), p. 338

notes.front: Protective systems for excavations more than {{c1::20}} feet deep must be designed by a registered professional engineer.
notes.explanation: Appendix F points such designs to 1926.652(b) and (c); the tabulated appendices cover excavations 20 feet deep or less.
notes.evidence: Protective systems for use in excavations more than 20 feet in depth must be designed by a registered professional engineer in accordance with § 1926.652 (b) and (c).
notes.source: 29 CFR 1926 Subpart P, Appendix F, Selection of protective systems, p. 370

notes.front: A sewer connection needs an excavation 24 feet deep in Type B soil. Who must design its protective system?
notes.choices:
A) A registered professional engineer
B) The competent person, using the Type B slope in Appendix B
C) The excavator operator
D) Anyone, if the trench is open less than 24 hours
notes.back: A: a registered professional engineer.
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: the appendix slopes apply only to excavations 20 feet or less deep. C has no design role in the rule. D is wrong: Appendix B's only short-term allowance is a steeper slope for Type A excavations 12 feet or less deep, and it does not change who designs deeper systems.
notes.explanation: At 24 feet the excavation is more than 20 feet deep, so its protective system must be designed by a registered professional engineer.
notes.evidence: Protective systems for use in excavations more than 20 feet in depth must be designed by a registered professional engineer in accordance with § 1926.652 (b) and (c).
notes.source: 29 CFR 1926 Subpart P, Appendix F, Selection of protective systems, p. 370

notes.front: According to the definition of sloping, the angle of incline needed to prevent a cave-in varies with which factors?
notes.back: Soil type, environmental conditions of exposure and the application of surcharge loads, among others.
notes.explanation: The definition says 'such factors as', so the list is open rather than complete.
notes.evidence: The angle of incline required to prevent a cave-in varies with differences in such factors as the soil type, environmental conditions of exposure, and application of surcharge loads.
notes.source: 29 CFR 1926.650(b), Definitions (excavations), p. 338

notes.front: Under Option (1) of 1926.652(b), with no soil classification, how steep may an excavation be sloped?
notes.back: No steeper than 1½ horizontal to 1 vertical (34 degrees from the horizontal).
notes.explanation: Option (1) also requires the configurations shown for Type C soil in Appendix B, the flattest of the soil types.
notes.evidence: Excavations shall be sloped at an angle not steeper than one and one-half horizontal to one vertical (34 degrees measured from the horizontal), unless the employer uses one of the other options listed below.
notes.source: 29 CFR 1926.652(b)(1), Design of sloping and benching systems, p. 341

notes.front: What are the maximum allowable slopes (horizontal to vertical) for simple slope excavations 20 feet or less deep in Type A, Type B and Type C soil?
notes.back: Type A ¾:1; Type B 1:1; Type C 1½:1.
notes.explanation: The weaker the soil, the flatter the slope Appendix B allows; stable rock, by definition, can stand with vertical sides.
notes.evidence: All simple slope excavations 20 feet or less in depth shall have a maximum allowable slope of 1:1.

image.alt: Four excavation faces drawn to scale: stable rock with a vertical face; Type A soil sloped three-quarters horizontal to one vertical; Type B soil sloped one to one; Type C soil sloped one and a half horizontal to one vertical.
image.credit: Drawn for this deck from 29 CFR 1926 Subpart P, Appendix B, Figure B-1, and the definition of stable rock in 1926.650

notes.source: 29 CFR 1926 Subpart P, Appendix B, Figure B-1.2, p. 350

notes.front: In Type A soil, a simple slope excavation 20 feet or less deep has a maximum allowable slope of {{c1::¾:1}}.
notes.explanation: Type A is the most stable soil type and has the steepest of the three maximum slopes. Figure B-1.1 allows a steeper ½:1 only for short-term excavations, open 24 hours or less and 12 feet or less deep.
notes.evidence: All simple slope excavation 20 feet or less in depth shall have a maximum allowable slope of 3⁄4:1.
notes.source: 29 CFR 1926 Subpart P, Appendix B, Figure B-1.1, p. 347

notes.front: In Type B soil, a simple slope excavation 20 feet or less deep has a maximum allowable slope of {{c1::1:1}}.
notes.explanation: Figure B-1.2 gives the same 1:1 maximum for benched Type B excavations of that depth.
notes.evidence: All simple slope excavations 20 feet or less in depth shall have a maximum allowable slope of 1:1. SIMPLE SLOPE 2. All benched excavations 20 feet or less in depth shall have a maximum allowable slope of 1:1
notes.source: 29 CFR 1926 Subpart P, Appendix B, Figure B-1.2, p. 350

notes.front: In Type C soil, a simple slope excavation 20 feet or less deep has a maximum allowable slope of {{c1::1½:1}}.
notes.explanation: This matches the Option (1) slope used when the soil is not classified.
notes.evidence: All simple slope excavations 20 feet or less in depth shall have a maximum allowable slope of 11⁄2:1.
notes.source: 29 CFR 1926 Subpart P, Appendix B, Figure B-1.3, p. 351

notes.front: Under Appendix B, what must happen to a slope that shows signs of distress?
notes.back: It must be cut back to an actual slope at least ½ horizontal to 1 vertical less steep than the maximum allowable slope.
notes.explanation: Normally the actual slope must merely be no steeper than the maximum; distress requires it to be flatter than the maximum.
notes.evidence: The actual slope shall be less steep than the maximum allowable slope, when there are signs of distress. If that situation occurs, the slope shall be cut back to an actual slope which is at least 1⁄2 horizontal to one vertical (1⁄2H:1V) less steep than the maximum allowable slope.
notes.source: 29 CFR 1926 Subpart P, Appendix B (c)(3), Actual slope, p. 346

notes.front: A competent person classifies the soil as Type C. The simple slope excavation will be 8 feet deep. At its maximum allowable slope, how far back from the toe must each face reach at the top?
notes.choices:
A) 12 feet
B) 6 feet
C) 8 feet
D) 4 feet
notes.back: A: 12 feet.
notes.choicesExplained: B uses the Type A slope (¾:1). C uses the Type B slope (1:1). D uses ½:1, a short-term slope that Appendix B allows only in Type A soil, for excavations 12 feet or less deep.
notes.explanation: Type C allows at most 1½ horizontal per 1 vertical, so 8 feet of depth needs 12 feet of horizontal run.
notes.evidence: All simple slope excavations 20 feet or less in depth shall have a maximum allowable slope of 11⁄2:1.
notes.source: 29 CFR 1926 Subpart P, Appendix B, Figure B-1.3, p. 351

notes.front: When may employees work on the faces of sloped or benched excavations at levels above other employees?
notes.back: Only when the employees below are adequately protected from falling, rolling or sliding material or equipment.
notes.explanation: The exception turns on whether those at the lower levels are protected from falling, rolling or sliding material or equipment.
notes.evidence: Employees shall not be permitted to work on the faces of sloped or benched excavations at levels above other employees except when employees at the lower levels are adequately protected from the hazard of falling, rolling, or sliding material or equipment.
notes.source: 29 CFR 1926.652(f), Sloping and benching systems, p. 343

notes.front: How far below the bottom of a trench support system's members may material be excavated, and on what conditions?
notes.back: Up to 2 feet, if designed for the trench's full-depth forces, with no sign of soil loss from behind or below the system.
notes.explanation: Both conditions apply: the design must cover the forces of the trench's full depth, and while the trench is open there must be no sign of soil being lost from behind or below the support system.
notes.evidence: 2 feet (.61 m) below the bottom of the members of a support system shall be permitted, but only if the system is designed to resist the forces calculated for the full depth of the trench, and there are no indications while the trench is open of a possible loss of soil from behind or below
notes.source: 29 CFR 1926.652(e)(2)(i), Support systems for trench excavations, p. 343

notes.front: Shields used in trenches are usually referred to as {{c1::trench boxes}} or trench shields.
notes.explanation: Shields may be permanent or portable, moved along as work progresses, and premanufactured or job-built.
notes.evidence: Shields used in trenches are usually referred to as ‘‘trench boxes’’ or ‘‘trench shields.’’
notes.source: 29 CFR 1926.650(b), Definitions (excavations), p. 338

notes.front: How far below the bottom of a trench shield may earth be excavated, and on what design condition?
notes.back: No more than 2 feet, and only if the shield is designed to resist the forces calculated for the full depth of the trench.
notes.explanation: The rule adds a second condition: no indications, while the trench is open, of a possible loss of soil from behind or below the bottom of the shield.
notes.evidence: Excavations of earth material to a level not greater than 2 feet (.61 m) below the bottom of a shield shall be permitted, but only if the shield is designed to resist the forces calculated for the full depth of the trench
notes.source: 29 CFR 1926.652(g)(2), Shield systems in trench excavations, p. 343

notes.front: When are employees not allowed inside a shield?
notes.back: While the shield is being installed, removed or moved vertically.
notes.explanation: Employees must also be protected from cave-ins when entering or leaving the areas the shield protects.
notes.evidence: Employees shall not be allowed in shields when shields are being installed, removed, or moved vertically.
notes.source: 29 CFR 1926.652(g)(1)(iv), Shield systems, p. 343

notes.front: A pipe crew in a trench box asks the excavator operator to lift the box a little so they can reach a joint below it. What does 1926.652(g) require?
notes.choices:
A) The crew may stay in if they hold on
B) One person may stay in to guide the box
C) Everyone must be out of the shield while it is moved vertically
D) The lift is allowed if it is under 2 feet
notes.back: C: everyone must be out of the shield while it is moved vertically.
notes.choicesExplained: A and B both leave employees in a shield being moved vertically. D confuses the 2-foot rule, which limits digging below a shield, not people inside one.
notes.explanation: A trench box is a shield, and no employee may be in a shield while it is installed, removed or moved vertically.
notes.evidence: Employees shall not be allowed in shields when shields are being installed, removed, or moved vertically.
notes.source: 29 CFR 1926.652(g)(1)(iv), Shield systems, p. 343

notes.front: In Appendix A, what is the hierarchy of soil and rock deposits, from most to least stable?
notes.back: Stable rock, Type A, Type B, Type C.
notes.explanation: Appendix A bases the categories on the deposits' properties and performance and on the environmental conditions of exposure.
notes.evidence: a method of categorizing soil and rock deposits in a hierarchy of Stable Rock, Type A, Type B, and Type C, in decreasing order of stability.
notes.source: 29 CFR 1926 Subpart P, Appendix A (b), Definitions, p. 344

notes.front: Type A soil is cohesive soil with an unconfined compressive strength of {{c1::1.5 tons per square foot}} or greater.
notes.explanation: Unconfined compressive strength is the load per unit area at which a soil fails in compression; Appendix A says it can be estimated in the field with a pocket penetrometer or thumb penetration tests.
notes.evidence: Type A means cohesive soils with an unconfined compressive strength of 1.5 ton per square foot (tsf) (144 kPa) or greater.
notes.source: 29 CFR 1926 Subpart P, Appendix A (b), Definitions, p. 344

notes.front: What are two conditions that stop a soil being Type A, however strong it is?
notes.back: Any two of: it is fissured; it is subject to vibration from heavy traffic or pile driving; it has been previously disturbed (among others).
notes.explanation: Appendix A also excludes soil in certain sloped layered systems and soil subject to other factors requiring a less stable classification.
notes.evidence: However, no soil is Type A if: (i) The soil is fissured; or (ii) The soil is subject to vibration from heavy traffic, pile driving, or similar effects; or (iii) The soil has been previously disturbed
notes.source: 29 CFR 1926 Subpart P, Appendix A (b), Definitions, p. 344

notes.front: Which soil that meets the Type A strength requirement is classified as Type B instead?
notes.back: Soil that meets the Type A strength or cementation requirements but is fissured or subject to vibration.
notes.explanation: Type B also takes previously disturbed soils, unless they would otherwise be Type C.
notes.evidence: Soil that meets the unconfined compressive strength or cementation requirements for Type A, but is fissured or subject to vibration
notes.source: 29 CFR 1926 Subpart P, Appendix A (b), Definitions, p. 345

notes.front: A stiff clay tests at 2 tons per square foot, but the trench runs beside a motorway and the soil is subject to vibration from heavy traffic. How is it classified?
notes.choices:
A) Type A, because of its strength
B) Stable rock
C) It cannot be classified
D) Type B
notes.back: D: Type B.
notes.choicesExplained: A is ruled out: no soil subject to vibration from heavy traffic is Type A. B is wrong: clay is soil, not rock. C is wrong: Appendix A places this soil in Type B.
notes.explanation: Soil that meets the Type A strength requirement but is subject to vibration is listed under Type B.
notes.evidence: Soil that meets the unconfined compressive strength or cementation requirements for Type A, but is fissured or subject to vibration
notes.source: 29 CFR 1926 Subpart P, Appendix A (b), Definitions, p. 345

notes.front: Type C soil includes cohesive soil with an unconfined compressive strength of {{c1::0.5 tons per square foot}} or less.
notes.explanation: Granular soils such as gravel, sand and loamy sand, and submerged or freely seeping soil, are also Type C.
notes.evidence: Type C means: (i) Cohesive soil with an unconfined compressive strength of 0.5 tsf (48 kPa) or less
notes.source: 29 CFR 1926 Subpart P, Appendix A (b), Definitions, p. 345

notes.front: A trench in a sandy loam has groundwater freely seeping from its walls. How should the competent person classify the soil?
notes.choices:
A) Type A
B) Type B, because sandy loam is listed there
C) Type C
D) Stable rock
notes.back: C: Type C.
notes.choicesExplained: B overlooks that soil from which water is freely seeping is Type C. A and D are more stable categories that seeping soil cannot meet.
notes.explanation: Appendix A lists soil from which water is freely seeping under Type C, whatever its texture when dry.
notes.evidence: Submerged soil or soil from which water is freely seeping
notes.source: 29 CFR 1926 Subpart P, Appendix A (b), Definitions, p. 345

notes.front: Under Appendix A, who classifies each soil and rock deposit, and on what minimum basis?
notes.back: A competent person, on the results of at least one visual and at least one manual analysis.
notes.explanation: The analyses may use the tests in Appendix A or other recognised methods of soil classification and testing.
notes.evidence: The classification of the deposits shall be made based on the results of at least one visual and at least one manual analysis. Such analyses shall be conducted by a competent person
notes.source: 29 CFR 1926 Subpart P, Appendix A (c)(2), Basis of classification, p. 345

notes.front: A foreman looks at a trench wall, decides the clay 'looks solid' and records it as Type A without handling any sample. What is missing under Appendix A?
notes.choices:
A) A registered professional engineer's signature
B) A laboratory test of every layer
C) Nothing, if the foreman is experienced
D) At least one manual analysis, alongside the visual one
notes.back: D: at least one manual analysis.
notes.choicesExplained: A is not required for classification. B goes beyond the rule, which accepts field analyses. C is wrong: experience does not replace the required manual analysis.
notes.explanation: Classification needs at least one visual and at least one manual analysis, conducted by a competent person; looking alone is only the visual half.
notes.evidence: The classification of the deposits shall be made based on the results of at least one visual and at least one manual analysis.
notes.source: 29 CFR 1926 Subpart P, Appendix A (c)(2), Basis of classification, p. 345

notes.front: When must the estimated location of underground utility installations be determined?
notes.back: Before an excavation is opened.
notes.explanation: The rule covers sewer, telephone, fuel, electric and water lines, and any other underground installation reasonably expected to be encountered.
notes.evidence: The estimated location of utility installations, such as sewer, telephone, fuel, electric, water lines, or any other underground installations that reasonably may be expected to be encountered during excavation work, shall be determined prior to opening an excavation.
notes.source: 29 CFR 1926.651(b)(1), Underground installations, p. 338

notes.front: Within what time must utility companies or owners be contacted and asked to locate their underground installations before excavation starts?
notes.back: Within established or customary local response times.
notes.explanation: The employer must also advise them of the proposed work, and the request comes before actual excavation starts.
notes.evidence: Utility companies or owners shall be contacted within established or customary local response times, advised of the proposed work, and asked to establish the location of the utility underground installations prior to the start of actual excavation.
notes.source: 29 CFR 1926.651(b)(2), Underground installations, p. 338

notes.front: A contractor plans to start digging a footing on Monday morning. Drawings show a gas line may cross the site. What must be done first?
notes.choices:
A) Dig by machine and stop if a pipe appears
B) Nothing, because the drawings already show the line
C) Determine the estimated location of the gas line before opening the excavation
D) Tell the crew to wear high-visibility vests
notes.back: C: determine the estimated location first.
notes.choicesExplained: A digs before the location is determined. B is wrong: the location must be determined, and the utility asked to establish it, before excavation. D does nothing about the buried line.
notes.explanation: A fuel line reasonably expected to be encountered must have its estimated location determined before the excavation is opened.
notes.evidence: The estimated location of utility installations, such as sewer, telephone, fuel, electric, water lines, or any other underground installations that reasonably may be expected to be encountered during excavation work, shall be determined prior to opening an excavation.
notes.source: 29 CFR 1926.651(b)(1), Underground installations, p. 338

notes.front: Trench excavations {{c1::4 feet}} or more deep must have a stairway, ladder, ramp or other safe means of egress within no more than 25 feet of lateral travel.
notes.explanation: Both numbers matter: the depth that triggers the rule and the maximum lateral travel to the nearest way out.
notes.evidence: A stairway, ladder, ramp or other safe means of egress shall be located in trench excavations that are 4 feet (1.22 m) or more in depth so as to require no more than 25 feet (7.62 m) of lateral travel for employees.
notes.source: 29 CFR 1926.651(c)(2), Means of egress from trench excavations, p. 339

notes.front: Workers are spread along a 6-foot-deep trench. One ladder stands at the end. A worker 40 feet away is laying pipe. Does the set-up meet 1926.651(c)(2)?
notes.choices:
A) No: that worker needs a means of egress within 25 feet of lateral travel
B) Yes: the rule only applies at 5 feet or deeper with no cave-in indication
C) Yes: one ladder per trench is enough
D) No: every trench needs a ramp, not a ladder
notes.back: A: no; egress must be within 25 feet of lateral travel.
notes.choicesExplained: C ignores the 25-foot limit. B mixes in the protective-system exception, which is a different rule. D is wrong: a ladder is an accepted means of egress.
notes.explanation: The trench is 4 feet or more deep, so a means of egress must be placed so no employee travels more than 25 feet laterally to reach one.
notes.evidence: A stairway, ladder, ramp or other safe means of egress shall be located in trench excavations that are 4 feet (1.22 m) or more in depth so as to require no more than 25 feet (7.62 m) of lateral travel for employees.
notes.source: 29 CFR 1926.651(c)(2), Means of egress from trench excavations, p. 339

notes.front: What must excavation workers exposed to public vehicular traffic be given and wear?
notes.back: Warning vests or other suitable garments marked with or made of reflectorised or high-visibility material.
notes.explanation: The employer must both provide the garments and have them worn.
notes.evidence: Employees exposed to public vehicular traffic shall be provided with, and shall wear, warning vests or other suitable garments marked with or made of reflectorized or high-visibility material.
notes.source: 29 CFR 1926.651(d), Exposure to vehicular traffic, p. 339

notes.front: Around excavations, where must employees not stand when lifting, digging or loading is going on?
notes.back: Underneath loads handled by lifting or digging equipment; and near any vehicle being loaded or unloaded.
notes.explanation: The rule names being struck by spillage or falling materials; operators may stay in cabs that give adequate protection.
notes.evidence: No employee shall be permitted underneath loads handled by lifting or digging equipment. Employees shall be required to stand away from any vehicle being loaded or unloaded to avoid being struck by any spillage or falling materials.
notes.source: 29 CFR 1926.651(e), Exposure to falling loads, p. 339

notes.front: When must the atmosphere in an excavation be tested before employees enter?
notes.back: When the excavation is more than 4 feet deep and oxygen deficiency or a hazardous atmosphere exists or could reasonably be expected.
notes.explanation: Subpart P gives landfill areas and areas where hazardous substances are stored nearby as examples, and defines oxygen deficiency here as less than 19.5 percent oxygen.
notes.evidence: Where oxygen deficiency (atmospheres containing less than 19.5 percent oxygen) or a hazardous atmosphere exists or could reasonably be expected to exist, such as in excavations in landfill areas or excavations in areas where hazardous substances are stored nearby, the atmospheres in the excavation shall be tested before employees enter excavations greater than 4 feet (1.22 m) in depth.
notes.source: 29 CFR 1926.651(g)(1)(i), Hazardous atmospheres, p. 339

notes.front: A 7-foot trench is being dug through an old landfill to lay a drain. What must happen before workers go in?
notes.choices:
A) Give each worker a dust mask
B) Wait one hour for gases to clear
C) Nothing, as the trench is open to the air
D) Test the atmosphere in the excavation
notes.back: D: test the atmosphere first.
notes.choicesExplained: B and C assume the air is safe without testing. A is not the test the rule requires, and a dust mask is not named as protection against oxygen deficiency.
notes.explanation: A landfill is the rule's own example of where a hazardous atmosphere could reasonably be expected, and the trench is more than 4 feet deep.
notes.evidence: such as in excavations in landfill areas or excavations in areas where hazardous substances are stored nearby, the atmospheres in the excavation shall be tested before employees enter excavations greater than 4 feet (1.22 m) in depth.
notes.source: 29 CFR 1926.651(g)(1)(i), Hazardous atmospheres, p. 339

notes.front: May employees work in an excavation where water has accumulated or is accumulating?
notes.back: Only if adequate precautions have been taken against the hazards of water accumulation.
notes.explanation: Subpart P says the precautions vary but could include special support or shield systems, water removal, or a safety harness and lifeline; a competent person monitors any water removal equipment.
notes.evidence: Employees shall not work in excavations in which there is accumulated water, or in excavations in which water is accumulating, unless adequate precautions have been taken to protect employees against the hazards posed by water accumulation.
notes.source: 29 CFR 1926.651(h)(1), Protection from water accumulation, p. 340

notes.front: Overnight rain leaves a foot of water in a trench, and more is seeping in. The crew is keen to finish a joint. Which option does 1926.651(h) accept?
notes.choices:
A) Work quickly before the level rises
B) Pump the water out, with the pumping monitored by a competent person, before work
C) Wait until the water drains naturally, however long it takes, with no inspection
D) Work in the water if boots are waterproof
notes.back: B: pump it out under a competent person's monitoring.
notes.choicesExplained: A and D put workers in accumulating water without adequate precautions. C skips the inspection a competent person must make after a rainstorm.
notes.explanation: Water removal is one of the precautions the rule names, and when it is used the equipment and operations must be monitored by a competent person.
notes.evidence: If water is controlled or prevented from accumulating by the use of water removal equipment, the water removal equipment and operations shall be monitored by a competent person to ensure proper operation.
notes.source: 29 CFR 1926.651(h)(2), Protection from water accumulation, p. 340

notes.front: Excavated materials and equipment must be kept at least {{c1::2 feet}} from the edge of an excavation, or held back by adequate retaining devices, or both.
notes.explanation: The purpose in 1926.651(j)(2) is to protect employees from materials or equipment falling or rolling into the excavation.
notes.evidence: Protection shall be provided by placing and keeping such materials or equipment at least 2 feet (.61 m) from the edge of excavations, or by the use of retaining devices that are sufficient to prevent
notes.source: 29 CFR 1926.651(j)(2), Protection from loose rock or soil, p. 340

notes.front: An excavator is piling spoil 1 foot from the edge of a trench, with no retaining device. What should the supervisor require?
notes.choices:
A) Pile it higher so it takes less room
B) Cover the pile with a tarpaulin
C) Keep the spoil at least 2 feet back from the edge, or use sufficient retaining devices
D) Keep the spoil at least 10 feet back
notes.back: C: at least 2 feet back, or retaining devices.
notes.choicesExplained: A and B leave the spoil able to fall or roll in. D is not the rule's figure; the minimum distance is 2 feet.
notes.explanation: Spoil at 1 foot is inside the 2-foot minimum, and no retaining device holds it back.
notes.evidence: Protection shall be provided by placing and keeping such materials or equipment at least 2 feet (.61 m) from the edge of excavations, or by the use of retaining devices that are sufficient to prevent
notes.source: 29 CFR 1926.651(j)(2), Protection from loose rock or soil, p. 340

notes.front: Who must inspect excavations, and when?
notes.back: A competent person: daily before work starts, as needed during the shift, and after every rainstorm or other hazard-increasing occurrence.
notes.explanation: The inspections cover the excavation, adjacent areas and protective systems, and are required only when employee exposure can reasonably be anticipated.
notes.evidence: An inspection shall be conducted by the competent person prior to the start of work and as needed throughout the shift. Inspections shall also be made after every rainstorm or other hazard increasing occurrence.
notes.source: 29 CFR 1926.651(k)(1), Inspections, p. 341

notes.front: What must happen when the competent person finds evidence of a possible cave-in or a failing protective system?
notes.back: Exposed employees must be removed from the hazardous area until the necessary precautions have been taken.
notes.explanation: The same applies to hazardous atmospheres and other hazardous conditions the inspection finds.
notes.evidence: exposed employees shall be removed from the hazardous area until the necessary precautions have been taken to ensure their safety.
notes.source: 29 CFR 1926.651(k)(2), Inspections, p. 341

notes.front: A shored trench was inspected at 7 a.m. At noon a heavy thunderstorm passes. The crew wants to go back in at 1 p.m. What does 1926.651(k) require?
notes.choices:
A) Nothing more: the daily inspection was done
B) An inspection by any crew member who is willing
C) A new design by a registered professional engineer
D) A fresh inspection by the competent person after the rainstorm
notes.back: D: a fresh inspection by the competent person.
notes.choicesExplained: A overlooks the after-rainstorm inspection. B is wrong: inspections are made by the competent person. C is not triggered by rain.
notes.explanation: Inspections must also be made after every rainstorm or other hazard-increasing occurrence, in addition to the start-of-work inspection.
notes.evidence: Inspections shall also be made after every rainstorm or other hazard increasing occurrence.
notes.source: 29 CFR 1926.651(k)(1), Inspections, p. 341

notes.front: Excavation versus trench: how do the two Subpart P terms relate?
notes.back: Every trench is an excavation; a trench is the narrow kind, generally deeper than wide and at most 15 feet wide at the bottom.
notes.explanation: Excavation covers any man-made cut, cavity, trench or depression formed by earth removal; the trench definition narrows it by shape and width.
notes.evidence: Excavation means any man-made cut, cavity, trench, or depression in an earth surface, formed by earth removal.
notes.source: 29 CFR 1926.650(b), Definitions (excavations), p. 337

notes.front: Shoring versus a shield system: what does each do, by definition?
notes.back: Shoring supports the sides of an excavation to prevent cave-ins; a shield withstands a cave-in's forces to protect the employees inside it.
notes.explanation: The definitions differ in their aim: shoring is designed to prevent the cave-in, while a shield is built to withstand one.
notes.evidence: Shield (Shield system) means a structure that is able to withstand the forces imposed on it by a cave-in and thereby protect employees within the structure.
notes.source: 29 CFR 1926.650(b), Definitions (excavations), p. 338
